facts.statement: Hyneria was a large predatory lobe-finned fish that lived in freshwater during the Famennian stage of the Devonian period.
facts.quote: Hyneria is a genus of large prehistoric predatory lobe-finned fish which lived in fresh water during the Famennian stage of the Devonian period.

facts.statement: The genus name Hyneria refers to the village of Hyner in Pennsylvania, near the site of the first fossil discovery.
facts.quote: The genus name Hyneria is a reference to the village of Hyner, Pennsylvania, near where the first specimen was found.

facts.statement: The species name H. lindae honors the wife of Keith Stewart Thomson, the scientist who first described the fish.
facts.quote: The species epithet H. lindae is derived from the name of the wife of Keith Stewart Thomson, who described this fish.

facts.statement: Keith Thompson discovered fossilized teeth, bones, and a fin of Hyneria in the Red Hill Shale of Pennsylvania in 1968.
facts.quote: En 1968, dientes fosilizados, huesos y una aleta fueron hallados por Keith Thompson en el Esquisto Red Hill de Pensilvania, Estados Unidos.

facts.statement: Despite many discoveries, a complete Hyneria skeleton has never been recovered.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, nunca se ha recuperado un esqueleto completo.

facts.statement: The type species H. lindae is estimated to have reached a total length of 2.5 to 3 meters.
facts.quote: H. lindae is estimated around 2.5 - 3 m in total length.

facts.statement: An isolated cleithrum suggests that some individuals of Hyneria were at least 2.7 meters long.
facts.quote: An isolated cleithrum AM 6545 likely belongs to an individual of at least 2.7 m in length.

facts.statement: While the largest complete jaw is 38 cm, a larger fragment exists that might belong to a jaw twice that size, though it may actually be from a rhizodont.
facts.quote: The largest complete jaw reaches 38 cm, but there is much larger fragment possibly from a jaw about twice that length, although that specimen may belong to a rhizodont instead.

facts.statement: If a large jaw fragment belongs to Hyneria, the animal could have reached lengths up to 3.5 meters.
facts.quote: Assuming this jaw fragment does pertain to Hyneria, and assuming proportions similar to more complete tristichopterids, it suggests H. lindae could possibly reach lengths up to 3.5 metres (11 ft).

facts.statement: Hyneria possessed a skull with heavy, ornamented dermal bones and a relatively long, shallow lower jaw.
facts.quote: Its skull had heavy, ornamented dermal bones and its lower jaw was relatively long and shallow.

facts.statement: Hyneria had stout teeth, including premaxillary fangs that were over 2 inches long.
facts.quote: The teeth were stout, with those of the premaxilla forming fangs upwards of 2 in.

facts.statement: The body of Hyneria was covered in cycloid scales.
facts.quote: Its body was covered by cycloid scales.

facts.statement: Hyneria had large sensory canals to help detect prey in the murky, low-visibility freshwater environments it inhabited.
facts.quote: It had large sensory canals to aid in detection of possible prey, as the freshwater environment it inhabited likely was murky and had low visibility.

facts.statement: Adult Hyneria retained juvenile skeletal features, suggesting they were likely neotenic.
facts.quote: Adult individuals retained juvenile features (i.e. partially unossified skeletons), suggesting that they were likely neotenic.

facts.statement: Hyneria could measure up to two meters in length and weigh up to half a ton.
facts.quote: Medía hasta dos metros de longitud, y llegaba a pesar hasta media toneladas.

facts.statement: Hyneria had powerful jaws and very sharp teeth, could swim very fast, and was a lethal predator.
facts.quote: Tenía potentes mandíbulas y dientes muy afilados, podía nadar muy rápido, convirtiéndole en un depredador letal.

facts.statement: In the TV series Walking with Monsters, Hyneria was depicted as a 5-meter female (twice its actual size) capturing prey by sliding in the mud like a walrus.
facts.quote: Se representaba a una hembra de Hyneria de 5 m (cuando solo medían 2) tratando de capturar presas resbalando en el barro como una morsa para capturar dos Hynerpeton

facts.statement: Hyneria fossils are found in the Catskill Formation of the Red Hill Shale, dating to the upper Devonian.
facts.quote: The fossils were found in the Catskill Formation of the Red Hill Shale, dating to the upper Devonian.

facts.statement: Hyneria lived during the Devonian period, approximately 360 million years ago.
facts.quote: Fue un depredador que vivió durante el Devónico, hace unos 360 millones de años.

facts.statement: The genus Hyneria was described by Thomson in 1968.
facts.quote: authority: Thomson, 1968

facts.statement: Hyneria belongs to the family Tristichopteridae.
facts.quote: familia: Tristichopteridae

facts.statement: Hyneria is classified within the superorder Osteolepidida.
facts.quote: superordo: Osteolepidida

facts.statement: Hyneria is a member of the class Sarcopterygii (lobe-finned fishes).
facts.quote: classis: Sarcopterygii

facts.quote: Hyneria is a genus of large prehistoric predatory lobe-finned fish which lived in fresh water during the Famennian stage of the Devonian period.

facts.statement: Hyneria was capable of swimming very fast, making it a lethal predator.
facts.quote: podía nadar muy rápido, convirtiéndole en un depredador letal.

facts.statement: It is debated whether a large jaw fragment found in the area actually belongs to Hyneria or to a rhizodont.
facts.quote: although that specimen may belong to a rhizodont instead.

facts.statement: Hyneria lived between 372.15 and 358.86 million years ago during the Famennian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Famennian to Famennian (372.15 to 358.86 million years ago)
